title: Metric learning and re-identification
summary: Learn embeddings where distance means identity: contrastive and triplet losses, semi-hard and batch-hard mining, ArcFace margins, and how re-ID is scored with rank-1, mAP and re-ranking.
outcomes: Explain why re-ID is open-set retrieval and why a closed-set classifier cannot answer it directly
Compute triplet losses and classify negatives as easy, semi-hard or hard for a given margin
Apply batch-hard mining on a P x K batch from its pairwise distance matrix
Compute ArcFace logits for a sample and explain what the scale s and the angular margin m do
Compute rank-1 and AP for a query under the Market-1501 cross-camera protocol

lessons.title: Why re-ID needs an embedding space, not a classifier

blocks.md:
A detector (previous course) gives you boxes around people in each camera frame. **Person re-identification** (re-ID) asks the next question: is the person in this crop from camera 1 the same person as that crop from camera 4?

The catch is that the people you must match at test time were never seen in training. In the Market-1501 benchmark, the 1,501 identities are split into disjoint training and test halves. A classifier with one output per training identity has no output for a new person, so it cannot answer the question directly.

Metric learning trains a network $f$ that maps an image to a vector (an **embedding**) so that distance encodes identity: crops of the same person land close together, crops of different people land far apart. Re-ID then becomes search.

- The **query** (also called probe) is the crop you want to match.
- The **gallery** is the set of crops to search, usually from other cameras.
- A **positive pair** shows the same identity; a **negative pair** shows two different identities.

For each query you rank the gallery by distance and hope the true matches come first.

blocks.title: From detector crops to a ranked gallery

scenes.caption: Each detected person crop goes through the same network f and comes out as one fixed-length vector.
Training: a metric loss looks at pairs or triplets of embeddings with identity labels and moves them closer or further apart.
Test: there is no classifier head. The query embedding is compared with every gallery embedding, so a person never seen in training still works.

blocks.md: The first loss built for this was the **contrastive loss** of Hadsell, Chopra and LeCun (CVPR 2006). Feed two inputs through the same network (a *siamese* setup), let $D$ be the Euclidean distance between their outputs, and let $Y = 0$ for a similar pair and $Y = 1$ for a dissimilar pair.

blocks.caption: Contrastive loss (Hadsell, Chopra, LeCun 2006). Similar pairs are pulled toward distance 0. Dissimilar pairs are pushed only while they sit inside the margin m.

blocks.title: Contrastive loss as a function of distance D

x.label: distance D between the two embeddings

scenes.caption: Similar pairs pay a cost that grows with distance, so the gradient always pulls them together.
Dissimilar pairs pay only when closer than m = 1. Beyond the margin the loss is exactly zero, so far-apart negatives stop contributing.
A larger margin m = 1.6 keeps pushing negatives until they are further apart, at the cost of more active pairs to satisfy.

blocks.prompt: Suppose you train with similar pairs only and drop the dissimilar term. What does the network learn?
blocks.reveal: **It learns to output a constant.** If every input maps to the same point, every distance is 0 and the loss is 0. Hadsell and colleagues note that minimizing over similar pairs alone usually leads to this collapsed solution, which is why the loss needs an explicit term for dissimilar pairs.

blocks.md: A subtle limit of contrastive loss: it pulls every same-identity pair toward distance 0, so it tries to squash all images of one person onto a single point. The FaceNet authors argued that a triplet loss is better suited, because it only asks same-identity images to be closer than other identities, letting one person's images spread out along a region.
Re-ID is open-set retrieval. You do not predict a label; you learn distances that rank true matches first for people the model has never seen.

blocks.question: A model trained on the Market-1501 training identities reaches high accuracy on held-out images of those same people. Why does that not tell you it will work for re-ID on Market-1501's test split?
options: Because the test images are smaller than training images
Because accuracy is not defined for embeddings
Because the test identities are different people, so what matters is whether distances generalize to unseen identities
Because re-ID only uses the gallery, never the query
blocks.explain: Re-ID test identities are disjoint from training identities. Closed-set accuracy on known people says little about whether the embedding separates new people. You need a retrieval evaluation on unseen identities.

blocks.question: With contrastive loss and margin m = 1, a dissimilar pair sits at distance D = 0.4. What is its loss?
blocks.explain: The dissimilar term is 0.5 x max(0, 1 - 0.4)^2 = 0.5 x 0.36 = 0.18. If the pair were at D = 1.2 the loss would be 0.

lessons.title: Triplet loss: the margin and easy, semi-hard, hard negatives

blocks.md: FaceNet (Schroff, Kalenichenko, Philbin 2015) trained face embeddings with a **triplet**: an *anchor* image $a$, a *positive* $p$ of the same identity, and a *negative* $n$ of a different identity. The goal is that the anchor is closer to every positive than to any negative, by at least a margin $m$ (the paper calls it $\alpha$).

blocks.tex: L(a, p, n) = \big[\, d(a,p) - d(a,n) + m \,\big]_+ \qquad [z]_+ = \max(0, z)
blocks.caption: Triplet loss. The loss is zero once the negative is at least m further from the anchor than the positive.

blocks.md:
FaceNet's details: the embedding is L2-normalized to unit length, $d$ is the **squared** Euclidean distance, the margin is $\alpha = 0.2$, and the embedding has 128 dimensions (the paper reports it can be quantized to 128 bytes per face). It reached 99.63% on the LFW face verification benchmark.

We use the toy below with plain (non-squared) Euclidean distance, as Hermans and colleagues do and as pytorch-metric-learning does by default; the ideas are the same.

**Toy batch.** Three identities A, B, C with two images each. Each embedding is a unit-length 2D vector at the given angle, so $(x, y) = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)$. A and B look alike (they sit near each other), C is far away. All distances in this course are computed from the exact angles and rounded to 3 decimals; gaps and losses are then computed from those rounded distances.

blocks.title: Six unit-length 2D embeddings (3 identities x 2 images)

scenes.caption: Six crops embedded on the unit circle. Labels: A1 and A2 are person A, and so on.
Anchor A1 at 0 degrees, positive A2 at 30 degrees. Their distance is d(A1, A2) = 0.518.
Person B sits just below A on the circle (a look-alike), while C is on the far side. Which negatives will produce a loss?

blocks.md:
With anchor A1, positive A2 ($d_{ap} = 0.518$) and margin $m = 0.2$, every negative falls into one of three bands:

- **Easy**: $d_{an} > d_{ap} + m = 0.718$. Loss 0, nothing to learn.
- **Semi-hard**: $d_{ap} < d_{an} < d_{ap} + m$. Further than the positive but inside the margin. Small positive loss.
- **Hard**: $d_{an} < d_{ap}$. The negative is closer than the positive. Large loss.

blocks.prompt: Before looking: of the four negatives B1, B2, C1, C2, how many give a non-zero loss for the triplet (A1, A2, n)?
blocks.reveal: **Two.** B1 at distance 0.347 is hard (closer than the positive), B2 at 0.618 is semi-hard (inside the 0.718 threshold), and both C images are easy. Half of the possible triplets already carry zero loss, even in this tiny batch.

blocks.title: Triplet (A1, A2, n) for each negative n, margin 0.2

scenes.caption: Distance from anchor A1 to each negative. The positive sits at 0.518 and the margin line at 0.518 + 0.2 = 0.718.
Loss = 0.2 + 0.518 - d(A1, n). B1 costs 0.371, B2 costs 0.100, the C images cost 0.

blocks.title: Triplet loss as the negative moves

scenes.caption: Left of d(a,p) is the hard band, between the two lines the semi-hard band, right of d(a,p) + m the easy band where the loss is flat zero.
Raise the margin to 0.5: the semi-hard band widens and more negatives become active. A margin that is too large makes the constraint hard to satisfy.

A tighter positive (d(a,p) = 0.3) shifts both lines left: B2 becomes easy and B1 only semi-hard (the dots keep their original losses). Pulling positives together helps as much as pushing negatives away.

blocks.md: Which negatives should you train on? Most random triplets are easy and give zero gradient, so FaceNet stresses that you must *select* triplets that violate the constraint. But the hardest ones are dangerous: FaceNet reports that selecting the hardest negatives can lead to bad local minima early in training and even a collapsed model ($f(x) = 0$). Their fix is **semi-hard** negatives, chosen online from within each mini-batch (around 1,800 images, with about 40 faces per identity).

Hard is not the same as useful. The very hardest negatives in a large dataset are often mislabeled or badly imaged examples (FaceNet names both). Training only on them teaches the network to fit noise.
A triplet only produces gradient when the negative is inside d(a,p) + m. Mining decides which of those active triplets you spend compute on.

blocks.question: Anchor-positive distance is 0.40 and margin is 0.2. A negative sits at 0.50. Which band is it in and what is the loss?
options: Semi-hard, loss 0.10
Easy, loss 0
Hard, loss 0.30
Semi-hard, loss 0.30
blocks.explain: 0.40 < 0.50 < 0.60, so the negative is further than the positive but inside the margin: semi-hard. Loss = 0.40 - 0.50 + 0.2 = 0.10.

blocks.question: Your triplet loss drops to near zero within the first epoch, but retrieval quality barely improves. What is the most likely cause?
options: The margin is too large
The learning rate is too small
Triplets are sampled at random, so almost all are easy and give no gradient
The embedding is L2-normalized
blocks.explain: Random triplets are mostly easy: the negative is already beyond d(a,p) + m, so the loss is zero regardless of how good the embedding is. A low loss here says nothing. Mine harder triplets.

lessons.title: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch

blocks.md:
Offline mining (embed a large chunk of the dataset with the current model, then search it for hard triplets) is slow: Hermans, Beyer and Leibe report training time growing from 7 h to 20 h in their experiments. Their 2017 paper *In Defense of the Triplet Loss for Person Re-Identification* moves mining inside the batch.

Build each batch from **P identities with K images each** (batch size PK). Then, for every image used as anchor, take its **hardest positive** (the furthest same-identity image in the batch) and its **hardest negative** (the closest other-identity image).

blocks.tex: \mathcal{L}_{BH} = \sum_{i=1}^{P}\sum_{a=1}^{K} \Big[\, m + \max_{p} D(x^i_a, x^i_p) - \min_{j \ne i,\, n} D(x^i_a, x^j_n) \,\Big]_+
blocks.caption: Batch hard triplet loss (Hermans et al. 2017). One term per anchor, so PK terms per batch. D is the plain Euclidean distance.

blocks.md: Our toy batch has P = 3 identities and K = 2 images, so each anchor has exactly one positive. Below is the full matrix of pairwise distances, the only thing batch hard needs.

blocks.title: Pairwise distances in the P = 3, K = 2 batch

scenes.caption: Each cell is the Euclidean distance between two embeddings (diagonal masked). Small values cluster in the A and B corner, where the look-alikes sit; A or B against C gives the largest values.
Anchor A1: the only positive is A2 at 0.518 (hardest positive by default).
Hardest negative for A1: the minimum over B1, B2, C1, C2 is B1 at 0.347. Loss = 0.2 + 0.518 - 0.347 = 0.371.
Anchor A2: positive A1 at 0.518, hardest negative B1 at 0.845. Already 0.327 beyond the positive, more than the 0.2 margin, so loss 0.
Anchor B1: positive B2 at 0.278, hardest negative A1 at 0.347. Gap is only 0.069, so loss = 0.2 - 0.069 = 0.131.
The other three anchors (B2, C1, C2) clear the margin. Only A1 and B1, the look-alike pair, drive learning in this batch.

blocks.title: Per-anchor losses: batch hard vs soft margin

scenes.caption: For each anchor, hardest positive distance minus hardest negative distance, read off the matrix. Positive means the negative is closer than the positive.
Hinge with m = 0.2: max(0, 0.2 + gap). Two non-zero terms; batch mean = (0.371 + 0.131) / 6 = 0.084.
Soft margin replaces the hinge with softplus ln(1 + e^gap). No term is ever exactly zero, so satisfied anchors keep pulling a little; mean 0.543.

blocks.md: The alternative, **batch all**, uses every valid triplet in the batch: $PK(PK - K)(K - 1)$ of them. Here that is $3 \cdot 2 \cdot 4 \cdot 1 = 24$ triplets, of which only 3 are active (A1-A2-B1 at 0.371, A1-A2-B2 at 0.100, B1-B2-A1 at 0.131). Averaged over all 24 the loss is 0.025; averaged over the 3 non-zero ones it is 0.201.

blocks.prompt: Hermans and colleagues found batch hard consistently beat batch all. Using the numbers above, why might averaging over all triplets hurt?
blocks.reveal: **The few useful terms get washed out.** With 21 of 24 triplets at zero, the mean loss (0.025) and its gradient are about 8 times smaller than the signal from the active triplets (0.201). The paper suggests exactly this and shows that averaging only the non-zero terms of batch all performs much better than the plain average.

blocks.md:
Two further findings from the same paper:

- **Soft margin.** Replacing the hinge $[m + \cdot]_+$ with softplus $\ln(1 + e^{x})$ gave the best scores in their comparison, and they used it for all later experiments.
- **Non-squared distance.** They noticed squared Euclidean distance made training more prone to collapsing, and that plain Euclidean distance keeps the margin interpretable as an actual distance.

Their pretrained **TriNet** (ResNet-50 with a 128-d embedding head, P = 18, K = 4, batch 72) reached 84.92% rank-1 and 69.14% mAP on Market-1501 single-query (with test-time augmentation).

blocks.code:
from pytorch_metric_learning import losses, miners, samplers

# P x K batches: m images per class, batch_size / m classes
sampler = samplers.MPerClassSampler(train_labels, m=4, batch_size=72)
loader = torch.utils.data.DataLoader(train_set, batch_size=72, sampler=sampler)

miner = miners.BatchHardMiner()              # hardest pos + neg per anchor
loss_func = losses.TripletMarginLoss(margin=0.2)  # library default margin is 0.05

for images, labels in loader:
    emb = model(images)                       # (72, 128)
    hard_triplets = miner(emb, labels)        # index tuples (a, p, n)
    loss = loss_func(emb, labels, hard_triplets)
    optimizer.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); optimizer.step()
blocks.caption: Batch hard with pytorch-metric-learning. Its miners default to L2 distance on normalized embeddings.

blocks.md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS in their supplementary material.
Sample P identities x K images so every batch contains positives and look-alike negatives, then mine within the batch. Mining becomes a max and a min over a distance matrix you already have.

blocks.question: In a P = 16, K = 4 batch with batch hard mining, how many triplet terms contribute to the loss?
blocks.explain: Batch hard produces one triplet per anchor, and every image in the batch is an anchor: P x K = 64 terms. The last option is the batch all count PK(PK - K)(K - 1).

blocks.question: You switch from batch hard to batch all without changing anything else and validation mAP drops. Which change would most directly test the 'washed out' explanation?
options: Increase the margin to 1.0
Average the loss only over triplets with non-zero loss
Square the distances
Use K = 1
blocks.explain: If zero-loss triplets dilute the gradient, averaging only the active terms removes the dilution. Hermans and colleagues ran this test and the non-zero average performed much better than the plain average.

lessons.title: ArcFace: putting an angular margin inside a classifier

blocks.md: A second family of methods trains a plain classifier over the *training* identities and then throws the classifier away, keeping the features for retrieval. No triplet mining is needed. The problem is that ordinary softmax only asks the correct class to win; it does not ask features of one identity to be tightly grouped, which is what retrieval on new identities needs.

ArcFace (Deng, Guo, Xue, Zafeiriou) fixes this in three steps:

1. Drop the bias and L2-normalize both the feature $x$ and every class weight $W_j$, so the logit is $\cos\theta_j$, where $\theta_j$ is the angle between $x$ and class $j$'s weight vector (its center direction).
2. Multiply all logits by a **scale** $s$, so features live on a hypersphere of radius $s$.
3. Add an **angular margin** $m$ to the angle of the true class only: the target logit becomes $s\cos(\theta_y + m)$.

blocks.caption: ArcFace loss. The paper uses s = 64, m = 0.5 radians (about 28.6 degrees) and 512-d features.

blocks.md: **Toy.** Reuse sample A1 (angle 0 degrees). Give the three training classes center directions $W_A$ at 15, $W_B$ at -28 and $W_C$ at 130 degrees. Then $\theta_A = 15$, $\theta_B = 28$, $\theta_C = 130$ degrees, and $\cos\theta$ = 0.966, 0.883 and -0.643. Use $s = 30$ and $m = 0.5$ rad.

blocks.prompt: With s = 30 and no margin, A1 is classified as A with probability 0.923 (logits 28.98, 26.49, -19.28). Now add m = 0.5 rad to A's angle only. Roughly what happens to p(A)?
blocks.reveal: **It collapses to 0.008 and the loss jumps from 0.080 to 4.789.** The target angle becomes 15 + 28.65 = 43.65 degrees, so the target logit drops to 30 cos(43.65 degrees) = 21.71, below B's 26.49. Plain softmax was satisfied because A1 is merely closer to A than to B. ArcFace demands that it be closer by a whole margin of about 28.6 degrees, so it keeps pulling A1 toward $W_A$ and away from $W_B$.

scenes.caption: Normalized softmax with s = 1: logits are just the cosines, all inside [-1, 1], so the right class barely wins (0.472 vs 0.434).
Scale s = 30, no margin: same angles, but logits 28.98, 26.49, -19.28 make A confident (0.923). The loss is only 0.080, so training would stop pushing.
ArcFace, s = 30, m = 0.5: target logit 30 cos(43.65 deg) = 21.71. Now B wins (0.992) and the loss is 4.789, a strong push to tighten the angle to A.

blocks.title: Target logit with and without the angular margin

scenes.caption: The margin shifts the target curve left by m: for the same angle, the true class gets a lower logit. A1's target logit falls from 28.98 to 21.71, under B's 26.49.
With m = 0 the two curves coincide and ArcFace is a normalized softmax.
The paper's setting s = 64: the gap between curves grows with s, so the same angular shortfall costs more. The dots stay at their s = 30 values.

blocks.md: Why an *additive angle*? The paper compares three margins on the normalized hypersphere: SphereFace multiplies the angle ($\cos(m\theta)$), CosFace subtracts from the cosine ($\cos\theta - m$), and ArcFace adds to the angle ($\cos(\theta + m)$). Because the angle on a unit sphere is a geodesic distance, ArcFace's margin is a constant gap in angle between classes, and the paper notes it trained without the extra tricks SphereFace needed to converge.

In pytorch-metric-learning, `losses.ArcFaceLoss(num_classes, embedding_size, margin=28.6, scale=64)` takes the margin in degrees. The class weight matrix is a learnable parameter of the loss, so you must give the loss its own optimizer.

The class weights only cover training identities. At test time you discard them and compare normalized features with cosine similarity, exactly as with a triplet-trained model. A large classification accuracy on training classes is not the goal.

blocks.question: Why does ArcFace need the scale s at all?
options: To make the margin m measured in degrees
With unit vectors the logits are cosines in [-1, 1], so softmax can never become confident; s widens the logit range
To keep the class weights from growing
To normalize the features to unit length
blocks.explain: Cosines are bounded by 1. With s = 1 and 3 classes, even the best case (cosine 1 to the true class, -1 to the others) gives p = 0.787. Scaling by s lets the probabilities approach 1 so the cross-entropy can be driven down.

blocks.question: A sample sits 20 degrees from its own class center and 35 degrees from the nearest other center. With m = 0.5 rad (28.6 degrees), is the ArcFace target logit above or below that other class's logit?
options: Above, because 20 < 35
Equal, because the margin cancels
Above, because the margin only applies to other classes
Below, because 20 + 28.6 = 48.6 degrees is larger than 35 degrees
blocks.explain: ArcFace compares cos(theta_y + m) against cos(theta_j). The effective target angle is 48.6 degrees, which exceeds 35 degrees, so the other class has the larger logit and the loss keeps pulling the sample toward its own center.

lessons.title: Measuring re-ID: rank-1, mAP, the Market-1501 protocol, re-ranking

blocks.md:
Re-ID is scored per query, on its ranked gallery list.

- **CMC rank-k** (cumulative matching characteristic): the fraction of queries with at least one true match in the top k. Rank-1 is the headline number.
- **Average precision (AP)**: walk down the list; at every true match record the precision so far (matches seen / position); average those over all true matches. **mAP** is the mean AP over queries.

blocks.caption: R is the number of true matches in the gallery, P(k) the precision of the top k, rel(k) is 1 if position k is a true match.

blocks.md: Zheng and colleagues introduced **Market-1501** (ICCV 2015) partly to argue for mAP: 1,501 identities, 6 cameras, 32,668 boxes from a DPM pedestrian detector (so misalignment and missing body parts are common), and 3,368 hand-drawn query boxes. Each query has on average 14.8 cross-camera ground truths, and CMC ignores all but the first. Search is **cross-camera**: gallery images of the query's identity from the *same* camera are marked **junk** and have zero influence on the score.
**Toy query.** Query A1 from camera 1, with our earlier embeddings. The gallery holds A1' (same person, same camera, angle 5 degrees), A2 (camera 2), A3 (camera 3, angle 70 degrees), B1, B2, C1, C2.

blocks.prompt: If you forget the junk rule and leave A1' in the gallery, what happens to rank-1 and AP for this query?
blocks.reveal: **Both look better than they should.** A1' is a near-duplicate frame at distance 0.087, so it ranks first: rank-1 is a hit and AP = (1/1 + 2/3 + 3/5) / 3 = 0.756. With the junk removed, rank-1 is a miss and AP is 0.500. Same-camera matches are easy because background and lighting match, which is exactly what the cross-camera protocol excludes.

scenes.caption: Gallery sorted by distance to the query. True matches are A1' (same camera), A2 and A3.
Without the junk rule: hits at positions 1, 3, 5 give precisions 1, 2/3, 3/5, so AP = 0.756 and rank-1 is a hit.
Market-1501 protocol: A1' shares the query's camera, so it is junk and removed. Look-alike B1 is now first: rank-1 is a miss.
Hits at new ranks 2 and 4 (positions 3 and 5 here): precisions 1/2 and 2/4, so AP = 0.500. CMC is a hit from rank 2 on.

blocks.question: System X ranks a query's 10 true matches at positions 1, 40, 41, ..., 48. System Y ranks them at positions 2 to 11. Which statement is right?
options: X has the better rank-1 and the better AP
Both have the same AP because both find all 10 matches
Y has the better rank-1, X the better AP
X has the better rank-1, but Y has a much better AP
blocks.explain: X's first match is at position 1, so rank-1 is a hit for X and a miss for Y. But X buries 9 matches around position 40, so its precision at those hits is low. AP is about 0.22 for X and 0.80 for Y. AP rewards finding all instances early, which is why Market-1501 reports mAP.

blocks.md: **Re-ranking with k-reciprocal neighbors** (Zhong, Zheng, Cao, Li, CVPR 2017) improves the list after the fact, with no extra training. Let $N(p, k)$ be the top-k neighbors of query $p$. A gallery image $g$ is a **k-reciprocal** neighbor if each is in the other's top-k:

blocks.tex: R(p, k) = \{\, g \mid g \in N(p, k) \;\wedge\; p \in N(g, k) \,\}
blocks.caption: A look-alike may be in the query's top-k without the query being in its top-k: its own true matches crowd the query out.

scenes.caption: Four images from the toy (junk A1' excluded). With k = 1 the query's nearest neighbor is the look-alike B1.
B1's own nearest neighbor is B2 at 0.278, not the query. So B1 is not a 1-reciprocal neighbor of A1: the match only runs one way.
A2 ranks second for the query, but A2's nearest neighbor is A1 itself. Mutual closeness is evidence of a true match that a single distance hides.
Simplified: the real method uses k around 20, expands the sets and compares whole neighborhoods with a Jaccard distance rather than single nearest neighbors.

blocks.md: The method expands each reciprocal set, encodes it as a weighted vector, computes a Jaccard distance $d_J$ between query and gallery neighborhoods, and blends it with the original distance: $d^* = (1 - \lambda)\, d_J + \lambda\, d$. On Market-1501 the paper uses $k_1 = 20$, $k_2 = 6$, $\lambda = 0.3$. The cost is that you need gallery-to-gallery neighbor lists, which grows with gallery size.

**Putting it together: a strong baseline.** Luo and colleagues (*Bag of Tricks*, 2019) showed that a ResNet-50 with global features, trained with ID loss (cross-entropy) plus batch-hard triplet loss (margin 0.3, P = 16, K = 4) and a few tricks, beats many more complex published methods. Each step below adds one trick on Market-1501.

blocks.title: Bag of Tricks on Market-1501, one trick at a time

scenes.caption: Rank-1 climbs from 87.7% to 94.5% with training tricks alone; BNNeck (a BatchNorm layer between the triplet feature and the classifier, cosine distance at test) is the largest single jump.
mAP moves more: 74.0% to 85.9%, then k-reciprocal re-ranking lifts it to 94.2% while rank-1 gains under 1 point. Re-ranking mostly recovers the matches lower in the list.

blocks.md: In-domain scores do not transfer. In the same paper, the full model trained on Market-1501 reaches only 27.5% rank-1 on DukeMTMC-reID, and random erasing, which helps in-domain, hurts cross-domain. New cameras, sites or seasons need their own evaluation.
Report mAP alongside rank-1, follow the cross-camera protocol, and compare methods only with the same tricks and the same re-ranking setting, because tricks alone can move rank-1 by about 7 points.

blocks.question: Your team wants to add k-reciprocal re-ranking to a live system that searches a gallery growing by millions of crops per day. What is the main concern?
options: It needs labeled data to retrain the model
It needs neighbor lists for gallery images too, so its cost grows with the gallery and must be recomputed as it changes
It only improves rank-1, never mAP
It only works with ArcFace features
blocks.explain: Re-ranking is unsupervised and needs no retraining, but it computes reciprocal neighbors from the gallery's own top-k lists. That is affordable on a fixed benchmark gallery and costly on a large, changing one.
